summary: Describes cryptographic algorithms and parameters that supplement the original Russian GOST specifications (GOST 28147-89, GOST R 34.10-94, GOST R 34.10-2001, and GOST R 34.11-94) for use in Internet applications. The document is informational.

eli5.summary: A country has its own recipe book of secret codes. This adds extra recipes and settings so internet programs can use them too.

questions: gost cryptographic parameters for internet use
how does gost key wrap work
what are the gost parameter sets
subtitle: The extra modes, key handling and parameter sets needed to use the Russian GOST algorithms on the Internet.

tldr.problem: The Russian GOST standards describe the basic algorithms but leave out much of what an implementation needs, such as a CBC mode, padding, key derivation, key wrapping and named parameter sets.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds CBC mode, three padding modes, CryptoPro key meshing, HMAC and PRF built on GOST R 34.11-94, VKO key derivation, two key wrap schemes, key diversification, and ASN.1 object identifiers for parameter sets.
tldr.outcome: It is a proposal from CRYPTO-PRO for the Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement community, and recommends using only the listed non-test parameter sets.

today: RFC 4357 is an Informational RFC. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the text says it is a proposal by CRYPTO-PRO rather than an Internet standard.

sections.title: What This Document Adds
sections.content:
The Russian standards GOST 28147-89 (a block cipher), GOST R 34.10-94 and GOST R 34.10-2001 (public key signatures) and GOST R 34.11-94 (a hash function) give basic information about how the algorithms work. Supplemental specifications are needed to use them effectively, and this document is a proposal from the CRYPTO-PRO company to provide them for the "Russian Cryptographic Software Compatibility Agreement" community.

Keys and initialization vectors are treated as little-endian when converted to or from byte arrays. The text defines helper functions such as encryptECB, encryptCFB, gostR3411 (a 256-bit hash) and gost28147IMIT (a 32-bit MAC).
sections.eli5: The original rule book says how the secret code works but not how to use it in everyday programs. This memo fills in the missing pages.

sections.title: Cipher Modes, Padding and Key Meshing
sections.content:
GOST 28147-89 defines only three modes: ECB, CFB and counter. This document adds CBC mode, in which each plaintext block is XORed with the previous ciphertext block (or the initialization vector for the first block).

For data that does not fill the 8-byte block, there are three padding modes: zero padding, PKCS#5 padding (an extra block of value 8 is added if there is no incomplete block) and random padding.

Key meshing changes the key after some amount of data, because a key should not protect more than 1024 octets in applications strictly robust to timing and EMI attacks. Null key meshing never changes the key. CryptoPro key meshing derives a new key and initialization vector every 1024 octets. Like OFB mode, it cannot resynchronize if encrypted data is corrupted, lost or reordered, so using it in protocols such as IPsec ESP needs special care.
sections.eli5: Chaining blocks together hides repeated patterns. Changing the key every so often is like swapping your padlock after each small box of letters.

sections.title: HMAC, PRF and Key Derivation
sections.content:
HMAC_GOSTR3411 is HMAC from RFC 2104 built on the GOST R 34.11-94 hash, with B = 32 and L = 32. PRF_GOSTR3411 is a pseudorandom function based on it, calculated as P_hash from Section 5 of the TLS specification.

The GOST standards define no key derivation, so the RFC adds VKO algorithms. They create a key encryption key (KEK) from one side's private key and the other side's public key, and both parties get the same value. VKO GOST R 34.10-94 hashes a Diffie-Hellman shared secret of 1024 bits into a 256-bit KEK. VKO GOST R 34.10-2001 does the same with elliptic curve keys and a 64-bit UKM. Both keypairs MUST have identical parameters, and each algorithm MUST NOT be used when a public key equals the generator or base point.
sections.eli5: Two people each combine their own secret with the other's public number and end up with the same shared key, without ever sending it.

sections.title: Key Wrapping and Diversification
sections.content:
Two key wrap algorithms encrypt a content encryption key (CEK) with a key encryption key. Both produce 44 octets: an 8-octet UKM, a 32-octet encrypted CEK and a 4-octet checksum (CEK_MAC). An unwrapper checks the length and the checksum and reports an error on a mismatch.

  • GOST 28147-89 Key Wrap encrypts the CEK directly under the KEK. It MUST NOT be used with a KEK from VKO GOST R 34.10-94, because that KEK is constant for each sender and recipient pair and encrypting many keys under it may reveal it.
  • CryptoPro Key Wrap first diversifies the KEK using the UKM, so it works with any KEK.

The CryptoPro KEK Diversification Algorithm builds a new key from a key and a 64-bit UKM in eight rounds. A separate secret key diversification algorithm (Section 7) derives a key from a secret key and 4 to 40 bytes of diversification data.
sections.eli5: Wrapping a key is like locking a small key inside a box with another key. A random tag mixed into the lock makes each box different.

sections.title: Parameter Sets and ASN.1 Identifiers
sections.content:
The GOST standards give no concrete parameter values, so the RFC names parameter sets with ASN.1 object identifiers. Section 8 explains what each set contains, and Section 11 lists the values:

  • GOST 28147-89: an S-box, a mode, a shift size and a key meshing algorithm. The sets are a test set and CryptoPro-A to D.
  • GOST R 34.11-94: an S-box and a start digest value.
  • GOST R 34.10-94: p, q and a, with p of 512 or 1024 bits.
  • GOST R 34.10-2001: elliptic curve coefficients, modulus, group order and base point.

All encryption sets use CryptoPro key meshing except the test set, which uses null key meshing. The appendices make up most of the document and hold the ASN.1 modules and long numeric tables.
sections.eli5: Each named setting is like a preset on a machine, so both sides can say 'use preset B' and know exactly what that means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC RECOMMENDs that software verify signature values, subject public keys and algorithm parameters against the GOST R 34.10 standards before use. Parameters affect how strong an algorithm is.

The non-test parameter sets were analyzed by a certification laboratory of the Scientific and Technical Center "ATLAS" and by the Center of Certificational Investigations. Using the test sets, or sets not described here, is NOT RECOMMENDED. If other parameters are used, the RFC recommends that an authorized agency examine them with approved methods of cryptographic analysis.
sections.eli5: The practice settings are only for practice. For real use, pick the settings that experts have already checked.
